paras: The Wilson registration beating was an attack in late July 1900 in the town of Wilson, North Carolina, in which "Red Shirts" beat an elderly Black man and his son "nearly to death" at a voter registration place. No deaths were reported, and the incident is known from a single sentence in a New-York Tribune dispatch that offered it as an example of Red Shirt intimidation of Black voters.

In the summer of 1900, during a North Carolina campaign that Democrats said "must be carried on Thursday next" at any cost, armed and mounted "Red Shirts" escorted the Democratic candidate for governor, Charles B. Aycock, from place to place. According to the Tribune's Raleigh correspondent, they gave "orders about negroes registering, about attending political speakings, and to stay away from the polls on Election Day."

In the week before the Raleigh dispatch of August 1, an old Black man went with his son to register at Wilson, and the registration official refused to register the son. The father remarked that the registrar "knew more about the age of his son than his father did." At that, the "Red Shirts" standing around fell upon the two men and beat them nearly to death. The report names neither the victims nor the attackers and does not say how many took part.
No report of an arrest, inquiry or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The beating appeared in the continuation of a long dispatch "by telegraph to the Tribune" from Raleigh, headlined "The 'Red Shirt' Terror of North Carolina," which ran on August 2. The dispatch set the Wilson case beside attacks on white Populist and Republican speakers and the claim, attributed to Democrats, that Red Shirts at registration places had kept at least 25,000 Black men from registering. Its correspondent concluded that "All semblance of a republican form of government has vanished" and compared the campaign to the Ku Klux era.
No other paper in either press was found carrying the Wilson incident.
